Intermediate: A lift accepts luggage weighing at most 20 kg. Write the comparison for a bag weighing w kg, and say whether 20 kg passes.
Use w <= 20. Exactly 20 kg passes because the limit includes equality.
A club admits a guest if they hold a valid ticket OR appear on the guest list. Lina is on the list with no ticket. What result should the predicate return, and why?
Return True. With or, either qualifying fact is sufficient, and Lina is on the guest list.
A warehouse clerk sees weights [2, 5, 8]. A filter keeps a weight only if it is greater than 2 and less than 8. Which weights survive? Explain the endpoints.
Only 5 survives. Both strict comparisons exclude their endpoints, 2 and 8.
The value 'False' arrived as form text. Why does if value still enter the yes branch, and what should the form parser do?
It is a nonempty string, so Python treats it as true. Parse the accepted text values explicitly into Boolean values before applying the predicate.
A library page lists available titles. Why should the predicate used to filter that list avoid subtracting a copy?
Filtering may call the predicate for every title or call it repeatedly. Keep the count unchanged while checking and deduct a copy only when a reservation succeeds.
Advanced: Two visitors each evaluate copies > 0 while the last copy is still available. Both see True. Why can two reservations succeed, and how would you prevent this?
They read the same old count before either write completes. Check and decrement in one atomic conditional update or transaction, and confirm exactly one row changed.
same/old count/concurrent/race
atomic/transaction/lock
A locker records weight as missing. A colleague defines too_heavy as weight > 5 and proposes accepting every parcel for which too_heavy is false. What decision is missing?
An unknown weight requires measurement or explicit rejection before comparison. A failed or unknown measurement does not establish that the parcel is within the limit.
unknown/missing
measure/reject/explicit
An engineer translates an in-stock rule into SQL WHERE quantity > 0. Why is a row with NULL quantity omitted? How would you produce a separate list of missing counts?
The comparison yields unknown for NULL, and WHERE retains only true rows. Use IS NULL to list missing quantities.
unknown/true
is null
A staff discount requires (member OR employee) AND purchase >= 100. A rewrite says member OR (employee AND purchase >= 100). Give a customer who exposes the error and the intended result.
A member who spends below 100 provides a counterexample. The intended rule rejects that purchase, while the rewrite accepts it based on membership alone.
member
below/under/less than/50/99

A data analyst uses a yes/no predicate to label training examples for a fraud model. The rule marks every payment above £100 as fraud. Why can a model score well on these labels and still miss real fraud?
The labels express the amount threshold, so reproducing it scores well. Evaluate against independently verified fraud outcomes, including smaller fraudulent payments.
threshold/amount/rule/labels
verified/independent/actual/confirmed
